course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

topic.title: The Compromise of 1850
topic.summary: How the question of slavery in the Mexican Cession brought a national crisis, what the Compromise of 1850 provided, and how Northerners and Southerners reacted to it.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: The Free-Soil Party, formed in 1848, was best known for its demand that
choices: slavery be ended at once in the states where it already existed
the settlers of each territory decide whether to allow slavery within its borders
slavery not be allowed to spread into the western territories
the United States pay slaveholders in order to free the enslaved people in the territories
questions.explanation: Free-Soilers wanted western land kept open to free workers and closed to slavery.
choiceExplanations: The party sought to stop the spread of slavery and not to end it in the states.
That was popular sovereignty.
Free-Soilers wanted western land kept open to free workers and closed to slavery.
The party did not propose payments to slaveholders.
questions.distinguisher: The immediate end choice is close because the Free-Soilers opposed slavery, but they sought to stop its spread and not to end it in the states.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Popular sovereignty was the idea that
choices: settlers in a territory should decide whether to allow slavery
Congress should ban slavery in every territory taken from Mexico
the president should decide the status of slavery in each new territory
each state should elect its senators by a direct vote of the people
questions.explanation: Senator Cass and later Senator Douglas argued that the people living in a territory should settle the question for themselves.
choiceExplanations: Senator Cass and later Senator Douglas argued that the people living in a territory should settle the question for themselves.
That was the Wilmot Proviso.
No one proposed leaving the choice to the president.
That change came with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913.
questions.distinguisher: The Congress ban choice is close because both ideas concerned the territories, but the Wilmot Proviso left the decision to Congress and popular sovereignty left it to settlers.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: California's request in 1849 to enter the Union as a free state caused a crisis mainly because
choices: its population was too small to qualify for statehood under the law
its admission would give the free states a majority in the Senate
Mexico had not yet accepted the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Congress had not yet decided to organize any territory in the Southwest
questions.explanation: The Senate had been evenly divided between free and slave states, and Southerners feared losing their veto over laws about slavery.
choiceExplanations: The Gold Rush had filled California with settlers.
The Senate had been evenly divided between free and slave states, and Southerners feared losing their veto over laws about slavery.
The treaty had been signed in 1848.
The crisis concerned the balance of power in the Senate.
questions.distinguisher: The population choice is close because California had been settled only recently, but the Gold Rush had brought enough people, and the dispute was about the balance in the Senate.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a provision of the Compromise of 1850?
choices: Slavery was abolished in Washington, D.C., and in the territory of Utah
Slavery was barred from all of the lands that had been taken from Mexico
The Missouri Compromise line was extended west to the Pacific Ocean
California entered as a free state, and a stronger Fugitive Slave Act was passed
questions.explanation: The Compromise admitted California as a free state, used popular sovereignty in Utah and New Mexico, and strengthened the Fugitive Slave Act.
choiceExplanations: Only the slave trade in the District of Columbia was ended.
Popular sovereignty applied in Utah and New Mexico.
The Compromise of 1850 did not extend the line.
The Compromise admitted California as a free state, used popular sovereignty in Utah and New Mexico, and strengthened the Fugitive Slave Act.
questions.distinguisher: The abolished in D.C. choice is close because the Compromise did affect the capital, but it ended only the slave trade there and not slavery itself.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850?
choices: Many Northerners were angered, and some states passed protective laws
Fewer people escaped from slavery, so Northern states stopped debating it
Accused fugitives gained the right to a jury trial in the free states
Southern leaders accepted the free status of California in return for the Act
questions.explanation: The Act required Northerners to help capture people who had escaped, and it turned many of them against the South.
choiceExplanations: The Act required Northerners to help capture people who had escaped, and it turned many of them against the South.
Escapes continued, and the Act increased the debate.
The Act denied them a jury trial.
Many Southerners still objected to California.
questions.distinguisher: The fewer escapes choice is close because the Act aimed to stop escapes, but Northerners resisted it and the debate over slavery grew.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a similarity between the Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850?
choices: Both banned slavery in the western lands north of the line at 36°30′
Both were struck down by the Supreme Court soon after they were passed
Both tried to settle the spread of slavery by an agreement between the sections
Both gave the settlers of each territory the right to decide the question of slavery
questions.explanation: Each compromise balanced free and slave states and sought to avoid a crisis over the territories.
choiceExplanations: Only the Missouri Compromise used that line.
The Court did not strike down either one at that time.
Each compromise balanced free and slave states and sought to avoid a crisis over the territories.
Only the Compromise of 1850 used popular sovereignty.
questions.distinguisher: The 36°30′ choice is close because the Missouri Compromise used that line, but the Compromise of 1850 did not.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between Northern and Southern attitudes toward the Compromise of 1850?
choices: Southerners objected most to the Fugitive Slave Act, and Northerners to California's free status
Northerners objected most to the Fugitive Slave Act, and many Southerners to California's free status
Northerners wanted slavery extended to Utah, while Southerners wanted it barred
Southerners opposed any federal law on slavery, while Northerners opposed only state laws
questions.explanation: Each section accepted parts of the Compromise and objected to the part that seemed to favor the other.
choiceExplanations: The objections were the reverse.
Each section accepted parts of the Compromise and objected to the part that seemed to favor the other.
Northerners did not seek to extend slavery.
Southerners welcomed the Fugitive Slave Act.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed choice is close because it names the same two provisions, but it gives each section the wrong objection.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The Nashville Convention of 1850, where some Southern delegates discussed leaving the Union, is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A dispute between South Carolina and President Andrew Jackson over the tariff
A call by Northern abolitionists for the Southern states to end slavery at once
A plan by Texas to leave the Union after the end of the Mexican–American War
Southern fears that a free California and the Wilmot Proviso threatened them
questions.explanation: Southern delegates feared that the free states would take control of Congress and limit the spread of slavery.
choiceExplanations: That dispute took place in 1832.
Delegates responded to national policy and to the Wilmot Proviso.
Texas did not seek to leave the Union.
Southern delegates feared that the free states would take control of Congress and limit the spread of slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The tariff dispute choice is close because Southern leaders had threatened to resist federal law before, but that dispute came in 1832.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) affected the debate over slavery by
choices: persuading Southern legislatures to pass laws that ended slavery gradually
convincing Congress to repeal the Fugitive Slave Act within a year
turning many Northern readers against slavery and the Fugitive Slave Act
showing that slavery had little effect on the lives of enslaved families
questions.explanation: The novel was widely read, and it made the human cost of slavery vivid to Northern readers.
choiceExplanations: Southern leaders rejected the book.
The Act remained in force.
The novel was widely read, and it made the human cost of slavery vivid to Northern readers.
The novel portrayed the cruelty of slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The repeal choice is close because the novel angered Northerners about the Act, but Congress did not repeal it until 1864.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.
